newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Sterling to push UK Jan input prices down.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Sterling to push UK Jan input prices down.

text.p: UK input prices are expected to have dipped further in January, with the strength of sterling helping to dampen import prices, economists said on Friday.

The data, due at 0930 GMT on Monday, will probably show inflationary pressures in the production sector staying mainly stable, with expected new year rises in factory gate output prices balancing out input weakness.
"We should see the subdued inflationary picture continue," said Philip Uglow, economist at Union Discount, who expects headline producer inflation to be unchanged at 1.7 percent.
A poll conducted by Reuters shows analysts expect a 0.4 percent month-on-month rise in output prices on a non seasonally adjusted basis, and a 1.6 percent rise on the year.

Input prices are expected to fall a seasonally adjusted 0.2 percent on the month and 5.7 percent on the year, while core output prices are forecast up 0.1 percent on the month and 0.8 percent on the year, unchanged from December.
January's figures will be a key signal for the rest of 1997, analysts said, with January price list rises likely to set the scene for higher output prices as the year progresses.
But the strong appreciation in sterling in the second half of 1996 will dominate Monday's figures.
"Things should carry on looking pretty benign in import prices for a while because of the strength of the pound, " said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel.
Sterling has gained around 14 percent on a trade-weighted basis since the summer of last year.

"We expect the feedthrough of sterling strength to impact on the producer output series in January -- with the underlying series forecast to show no increase, despite the recent increase in the CBI expected price balance," said Michael Lewis at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, who left interest rates unchanged at his last monetary meeting on Wednesday, should draw comfort from the subdued pipeline inflation scenario expected from Monday's figures.
Clarke is keen not to tighten monetary policy until after the election, due sometime before May 22.
Effects of increased duty charges from last November's budget may also exert upward pressure on output prices, analysts said, although the effect was likely to be small.
"The budget effects due to come through in December didn't really show through," said Cole. "We may get more in January."
